questions.story:
"The Ashfield Line"

Passage 1
The Ashfield Line has carried passengers between the town and the city since 1954. For most of that time it ran four trains an hour, and the platform clock at Ashfield station was wound by hand every Monday morning by the same stationmaster for thirty-one years. The waiting room still has its original wooden benches. Around nine thousand people use the line each week, and the timetable board at the entrance has not been replaced since the station was refurbished in 1988.

Passage 2
In 2016 the operator replaced the line's ageing signal system with a digital network. Because the new software had been tested only on straight track, it struggled with the tight curve outside Ashfield tunnel. As a result, signals began switching to red without any train being present. Drivers were instructed to stop and wait for clearance each time this happened, and consequently a journey that had once taken twenty-eight minutes now regularly took over fifty.

Passage 3
These delays led to problems the operator had not foreseen. Passengers began missing connections at the city terminus, which caused complaints to rise from twelve a month to over four hundred. Season ticket sales fell by nineteen per cent within a year, resulting in reduced income for the operator. Two morning services were withdrawn to save money, and the loss of those trains made overcrowding on the remaining services considerably worse than before.

Passage 4
The operator now faces a genuine difficulty. Replacing the digital system entirely would cost an estimated forty million pounds, a sum the company does not have and cannot borrow at current rates. Yet leaving the faulty signals in place risks losing the remaining passengers altogether, and the regulator has warned that the line's operating licence will be reviewed next year. The challenge is to restore reliability quickly, without the money that a full replacement would require.

Passage 5
In 2024 the operator resolved on a partial answer. Engineers rewrote the software governing the tunnel curve alone, leaving the rest of the network untouched, at a cost of two million pounds. False red signals at that location have since fallen by eighty-four per cent, and journey times have shortened to thirty-four minutes. Nevertheless, three other curves on the line remain unmodified, and the regulator has not yet confirmed whether this will satisfy next year's review.

Passage 6
Two repair strategies were weighed before the decision. A full system replacement fixes every fault at once and needs no further work for twenty years. Partial rewriting, on the other hand, costs a fraction of that sum but must be repeated curve by curve as problems appear. Both approaches restore safe running, and both have been adopted by other operators facing similar faults. Unlike full replacement, however, partial rewriting can be funded from existing budgets without new borrowing.

options.text: Compare and Contrast

The passage uses no recognisable structure
